title: The Gardener of Forgotten Graves
summary: An old gardener tends the graves no one visits anymore, keeping the forgotten dead company. When Yara learns that a grave, once remembered again, can call its sleeper partway back, she wants to wake her grandmother — and must weigh what the living owe the dead against what the dead need from the living.

chapters.title: The Graves No One Visits
chapters.body:
There is a particular sadness to a forgotten grave, and the old gardener of Barrow Hill had made it his life's work to ease it.

He tended the cemetery on the hill above the town of Millrace — but not the way an ordinary groundskeeper does, mowing and trimming and moving on. He tended it the way you tend the lonely. The new graves, the ones still visited, still wept over, still heaped with fresh flowers — those he left mostly alone, because they had the living to care for them. It was the old graves he gave his heart to. The ones whose visitors had themselves grown old and died. The ones whose names had worn off the stones. The ones no one living remembered at all — the truly forgotten dead, whose graves sat untended in the far corners of the hill, sunken and moss-covered and alone.

Those graves, the old gardener tended with special love. He cleared the moss so the faded names could be read. He planted flowers on the sunken mounds. He learned what he could of who they'd been, from the old parish records, and he spoke their names aloud as he worked, so that the names would be said by someone, at least, even if only him. “Good morning, Tomas Ashfield,” he would say, kneeling by a two-hundred-year-old stone. “Good morning, Bess who was a weaver. I remember you. Someone remembers you.” Because he believed — and he was old enough and wise enough to be right — that the worst thing about being dead was not the dying. It was being forgotten. And he had made himself the one who did not forget.

Yara was thirteen, and she came to the cemetery to visit her grandmother, who had died the year before, and that was how she met the old gardener.

She found him tending a forgotten grave in the far corner, speaking a stranger's name aloud with great tenderness, and she watched him for a while, and then she asked what he was doing. And the old gardener, glad of company, told her about his work — about the forgotten dead, and the sadness of being unremembered, and how he made himself the keeper of names no one else kept.

Yara thought it was the kindest thing she'd ever heard. But she also had a grief of her own, fresh and sharp, and being in the cemetery had stirred it, and after a while she said, quietly: “I wish I could do more than remember my grandmother. Remembering isn't enough. I miss her so much. I'd give anything to have her back — even just for a little while. Even just to say the things I didn't get to say.”

And the old gardener grew very still. And he looked at Yara for a long moment, with an expression she couldn't read — something caught between pity and warning. And then he said, slowly, as if the words themselves were dangerous: “Be careful what you wish for, child. Because there is a thing I've learned, tending these graves all these years, that most people never learn. And it's this: a grave, once truly remembered again — remembered hard enough, wished-for hard enough — can call its sleeper partway back. The dead are not as far away as people think. And the forgotten ones... the forgotten ones are always listening for their names. Which is a mercy. And also, sometimes, a terrible danger.”

chapters.title: What the Dead Need
chapters.body:
Yara made the old gardener explain, and though he clearly wished he hadn't spoken, he did, because he could see she would not let it go.

“The dead sleep,” he said. “That's the truth of it. Not gone — sleeping. And a sleep is a restful thing, a peaceful thing, if you're allowed to sink into it fully. The forgotten dead, the ones I tend — the sad thing is not that they're asleep. It's that they've been left to sleep alone, with no one to have said a kind goodbye, no one to visit, no one to remember they were ever awake. So I keep them company. I say their names. I let them know, in their sleep, that they mattered. That's all the dead truly need from the living, child: to be remembered kindly, and then to be let sleep.” He paused. “But there's a thing the living can do, if they can't bear to let go. If you remember a grave's sleeper hard enough — not kindly, but hungrily, wishing them back with all your might, refusing to let them sink into their sleep — you can call them partway up out of it. Not all the way alive. But partway. A shade. A presence. Enough to speak with, for a while. Enough to feel they're near.”

Yara's heart leapt. “Then I could — my grandmother — I could call her back? Partway? Just to talk to her again?”

“You could,” the old gardener said heavily. “Many have. It's the most natural wish in the world, for someone grieving. But listen to me, child, because this is the part that matters.” He knelt to her level. “When you call a sleeper partway back, you take them out of their rest. And they cannot be both — cannot be half-awake for you and fully at rest at the same time. Every hour you hold your grandmother partway up out of her sleep, to comfort yourself, is an hour she cannot sink into the peace the dead are owed. You'd be keeping her on the cold stairs between sleeping and waking — not alive, which she can't be again, but not resting either. Held there. For you. Because you couldn't bear to let her go.” His voice was very gentle, and very sad. “And the dead love us, child. That's the cruelty of it. A called-back grandmother will stay, if you ask her to. She'll stay on those cold stairs for years, denying herself her rest, because she loves you and can't bear your grief any more than you can bear her absence. So she'll linger, half-here, neither alive nor resting, growing thinner and colder and more tired — all to comfort a grief that never heals because you never let it. I've seen it. A woman kept her husband called-back for thirty years. She was never comforted — you can't be, it's not real comfort, it's just postponed grief. And he was never at rest. Two people, one alive and one dead, both trapped on the stairs between, because she could not say goodbye.”

Yara was quiet, her leaping heart sinking.

“That's why I only say their names kindly,” the old gardener went on, gesturing at the forgotten graves around them. “I remember them — but I remember them to honor them, and to let them rest, not to hold them. There's a world of difference between remembering someone so they can sleep in peace, knowing they mattered, and remembering someone so hard you drag them up out of their peace to soothe yourself. The first is love. The second is love too — but love turned to clutching, and clutching, even loving clutching, is a cruelty to the one you clutch. The kindest thing you can do for your grandmother, child, is the hardest thing: to remember her with all your heart, and to let her sleep.”

But Yara, thirteen and grieving and aching to say the things she'd never said, looked out over the graves, and was not sure she was strong enough to be that kind.

chapters.title: The Kindest Goodbye
chapters.body:
That night, Yara went back to the cemetery alone, to her grandmother's grave, to decide.

She knelt at the stone in the dark, and she felt how close her grandmother was — the old gardener had been right, the dead were not as far as people thought — and she felt that if she only remembered hard enough, wished hard enough, refused hard enough to let go, she could call her grandmother partway up out of sleep, and speak with her again, and not be so terribly alone.

And oh, she wanted to. She wanted to say the things she hadn't said — that she loved her, that she was sorry for the childish crossness of their last days, that she missed her every hour. She wanted to hear her grandmother's voice again, just once, just for a while. The wish was so strong it shook her. She began, almost without deciding to, to remember her grandmother hungrily — to reach for her, to pull — and she felt something stir in the grave below, felt her grandmother begin, sleepily, lovingly, to answer the call and rise toward her.

And it was that — the feeling of her grandmother beginning to wake, beginning to leave her rest, out of love, to comfort her — that stopped Yara.

Because she understood, in that moment, what the old gardener had truly been telling her. Her grandmother would come. That was the terrible thing. Her grandmother loved her, and would rise up out of her well-earned rest, and linger on the cold stairs between sleeping and waking for as long as Yara needed her — years, maybe, growing thinner and colder and more tired, denying herself peace, all to soothe a granddaughter who couldn't say goodbye. And Yara would never truly be comforted, because it wouldn't be real, only postponed. Two people trapped on the stairs, one grieving and one dead, because Yara loved her grandmother so much she couldn't bear to let her rest.

And Yara realized that this was the last gift she could give her grandmother, and the hardest, and the truest. Not to call her back. To let her go. To love her enough to want her at peace more than she wanted her own comfort. To remember her — fiercely, forever — but to remember her kindly, the gardener's way, so her grandmother could sink fully into her rest knowing she had mattered, and been loved, and been let go with love.

So Yara did not pull. She stopped reaching hungrily, and instead she did the kind thing. She laid her hand on the cold stone, and she felt her grandmother poised there, half-risen, waiting to see if she'd be called all the way up — and Yara said, through her tears, the goodbye she'd been too late to say the first time:

“Grandma. It's me. I'm sorry I didn't get to say goodbye before. I'm sorry for the silly things, at the end. I love you. I love you so much, and I miss you every single day, and I'm going to remember you for my whole life — everything you taught me, the way you laughed, the way you said my name. You mattered. You matter. You're not forgotten, and you never will be, not while I'm alive.” She pressed her hand to the stone. “But I'm not going to call you back. I know you'd come. I know you'd stay, for me. And that's exactly why I won't ask you to. You've earned your rest. Go and sleep, Grandma. Sleep deep and peaceful, and know that you were loved, and that you're remembered, and that I'm going to be all right. Go on. I've got it from here.”

And she felt her grandmother — poised on the cold stairs, half-risen out of love — settle back down. Not dragged, not banished. Released. She felt her grandmother sink, gently and gratefully and at peace, down into the full deep rest of the kindly-remembered dead, carrying with her, into that rest, the goodbye and the love and the certainty of being remembered. And it did not feel like losing her again. It felt like finally, properly, letting her arrive somewhere good.

Yara wept at the grave for a long time. But it was a different weeping than the hungry, clutching grief that had brought her there. It was the clean grief of a true goodbye — the kind that hurts, and heals, because it lets both people go free: the dead into their rest, and the living into their life.

She went to find the old gardener in the morning, and told him what she'd done, and the old man's weathered face filled with a deep and quiet approval. “You did the hardest thing,” he said. “And the kindest. Most people can't. Most people clutch.” He looked out over his forgotten graves. “You gave your grandmother the two things the dead truly need — to be remembered, and to be let rest. That's the whole of it. That's all any of us can give them.”

And Yara, who had come to the cemetery wanting to wake the dead, stayed — not that day, but in the years after — to help the old gardener tend it. She learned to clear the moss and plant the flowers and read the faded names, and to say them aloud, kindly, so the forgotten dead would know they mattered. And when the old gardener himself finally died, it was Yara who tended his grave, and spoke his name, and remembered him — kindly, and let him rest. Because she had learned the deepest thing the cemetery had to teach: that we owe the dead our memory, fierce and lasting and full of love. But we owe them, too, their peace. And the truest love is not the love that clutches and calls them back, but the love that remembers them with all its heart, and says the goodbye, and lets them sleep.
